title: The Remnants: Corponation Sovereignty and the World Outside the Network
body:
# The Remnants: Corponation Sovereignty and the World Outside the Network

## The Vocabulary

The world outside the GLMZ goes by several names, and the name a person uses reveals something about them.

**Remnants** is the neutral term — used in academic and administrative contexts, used by people in those places to describe themselves without irony or apology, used in the GLMZ when precision matters more than tone. It describes accurately: what remains after the reorganization. The Remnants are not a concept the corponations invented; it is a concept the situation produced. Things remained. They became the Remnants.

**The Gap** is the GLMZ term — the one used without thinking by people who have never left the Corridor, the one that reveals the speaker's coordinates without them intending to reveal anything. The origin is Pulse transit culture. The automated announcement at Chicago Station says: *Mind the Gap* — and the joke, among people who have done the Chicago-to-Rotterdam run, is that the Gap is a thousand little towns at Mach 6. You pass through them in forty-three minutes. You do not stop. The Pulse doesn't stop. There are no windows. You emerge in Rotterdam and the thousand towns are gone as completely as if they had not existed. The Gap is the name for the experience of being between nodes, and it has become, by extension, the name for everything that isn't a node. The word is not cruel in the mouths of most people who use it. It is simply inaccurate in the way that comfortable assumptions are inaccurate: the Remnants are not only the space between GLMZ nodes. They are also, for approximately 800 million people, home.

**The Old World** is a different register entirely — nostalgic, slightly romantic, used by people who study history and by people who have visited, used with different emotional valences depending on whether the speaker admires what the Remnants preserved or mourns what they lost. The Old World is where the pre-corponation social structures persisted: democratic governments that still hold elections where the elections mean something, communities organized around geography rather than corporate affiliation, legal systems derived from the same frameworks that once governed the GLMZ before the regulatory collapse. Some people find this charming. Some find it quaint. Some find it genuinely preferable. Very few people move from the GLMZ to the Old World, but some do, and the ones who do tend to find it impossible to explain to the ones who didn't.

## How Governments Stopped

The corponation era did not begin when governments fell. It began when governments became optional.

The municipal and state governments of the former United States did not all collapse simultaneously or for the same reasons. The collapse was a spectrum: some governments failed quickly and catastrophically (the Illinois state government's 2131 insolvency, the formal dissolution of California's infrastructure authority in 2118) while others degraded slowly, maintaining the forms of function without the substance. What they shared was the same underlying mechanism: the tax base contracted as the economically productive activity moved to corponation sovereign territory, which was not subject to municipal or state taxation; the services that tax revenue funded became increasingly unreliable; the political constituency for maintaining those services contracted as the people who depended on them moved to corponation territory where they had access to corponation services; the government became an institution that served an ever-smaller population with ever-fewer resources.

At a certain point — and the point was different for each jurisdiction, and was usually not marked by any formal declaration — the government stopped being the relevant institution in people's lives. The school systems still operated, technically, because no one had formally closed them, but the teachers had left for corponation employment and the students had moved with their families into corponation territory. The police departments still operated, technically, because no one had formally disbanded them, but the funding had been redirected and the officers had taken corponation security contracts and the function of public order had migrated to Arcturus Civil Security and its regional equivalents, who charged for their services and collected from the corponations that wanted order in their territories and provided nothing to everyone else.

The corponations did not defeat governments. They rendered them unnecessary in the places where corponations operated, and withdrew from the places where they did not operate, and what was left — the places that were neither corponation territory nor adjacent to it — was the Remnants.

## What the Remnants Are

The Remnants are the majority of the land surface of the former United States. The corponations claimed what they could profit from: the lakefront, the rail corridors, the major production facilities, the infrastructure with high return on investment. They did not claim the coal country of Appalachia, where the coal was gone. They did not claim the rural Midwest, where the agricultural margins were insufficient to justify the administrative costs of sovereignty. They did not claim the post-coastal cities, where the infrastructure investment required to operate was greater than the economic return available. These places remained. They are the Remnants.

The Remnants are not apocalyptic. This is the most common misunderstanding, perpetuated by GLMZ entertainment content that cannot portray the outside world without either romanticizing it into a pastoral idyll or dramatizing it into catastrophe. The actual Remnants are neither. They are places where people live, where communities function, where the ordinary processes of human life continue — food, shelter, relationship, work, culture, governance — through means that predate and postdate the corponation era. Democratic governments still operate in the Remnants, because there is no corponation to preempt them. Municipal services still exist, funded by municipal taxes collected from municipal populations, on the model that worked for two centuries before the corponation era made it unnecessary in the places the corponations wanted.

The Remnants lack what the GLMZ has: the Pulse, the tier-classification social mobility framework, the advanced medical and augmentation technology that is locked behind corponation territorial access, the infrastructure investment that has made the Corridor one of the most densely serviced environments in human history. These are significant absences. They are not the same as the absence of civilization.

## The GLMZ's Relationship to the Remnants

The GLMZ regards the Remnants the way the center of anything regards its periphery: with indifference, interrupted occasionally by economic interest.

The corponations buy from the Remnants. Agricultural products from the Midwestern Remnants, raw materials from the Appalachian resource territories, fish and timber from the coastal Remnants — all of these flow into the GLMZ through trade arrangements that are profitable for the corponations and sustaining for the Remnant communities that participate in them. The trade is asymmetric. It is not exploitation, exactly, in any legally definable sense. It is simply the trade between a party with many options and a party with few, negotiated accordingly.

The GLMZ occasionally sends people to the Remnants: researchers, resource surveyors, the occasional journalist interested in the contrast, and — more quietly — the corponation representatives who manage the supply agreements. These people go to the Remnants and return with materials, data, and the particular quality of experience that comes from visiting a place that does not know what tier you are. In the Remnants, tier means nothing. The GLMZ social order stops at the corponation border, and the corponation borders stop where the Remnants begin.

Some GLMZ residents find this terrifying. Some find it liberating. Most find it impossible to seriously contemplate for longer than the duration of an interesting thought, because the alternative to the GLMZ social order is the Remnants, and the Remnants, for all their interest, are not the Pulse and not the Grand Exchange and not the lakefront and not the world that the GLMZ has made — the world that, whatever its qualities, is the only world that most GLMZ residents have ever inhabited or intend to.
